Domains: Cell biology — mitochondrial energy production
🎭 Janusian🗺️ Frontier Research Group💀 Refuted🔬 Actively Researched

Score breakdown (+30 pts)

  • Phase 1 self-report (4/5): not scored — near-zero predictive signal, see Failure 5
  • Phase 2 ADJACENT_ACTIVE: +30
  • Adversarial refutation REFUTED, unanimous (0-of-3 survive): -15
  • independently confirmed (3 separate agents, full agreement)
  • Actively researched, most recent evidence 2023 (3y old): +15

🔬 Independent Research Matches

The cited studies provide evidence that mitochondrial energy production can be both efficient and inefficient under the same cellular conditions, supporting the proposed theory and its falsifiable prediction.

  • High efficiency versus maximal performance—the cause of oxidative stress in eukaryotes: a hypothesis (2013) — Bernhard Kadenbach, Rabia Ramzan, Sebastian Vogt
    This study discusses the dual nature of mitochondrial efficiency, proposing that both high efficiency and maximal performance can coexist, leading to oxidative stress under certain conditions.
  • High phosphorylation efficiency and depression of uncoupled respiration in mitochondria under hypoxia (2000) — Erich Gnaiger, Gabriela Méndez, S C Hand
    This research examines mitochondrial efficiency under hypoxic conditions, observing both high phosphorylation efficiency and reduced uncoupled respiration, indicating simultaneous efficient and inefficient energy production.
  • Mitochondrial temperature homeostasis resists external metabolic stresses (2023) — Mügen Terzioglu, Kristo Veeroja, Toni Montonen, et al.
    This study investigates mitochondrial temperature regulation under metabolic stress, providing evidence that mitochondria can maintain both efficient and inefficient energy production simultaneously.

Notes

These sources provide evidence that mitochondrial energy production can be both efficient and inefficient under the same conditions, supporting the hypothesis that cells under metabolic stress may exhibit ATP yields that are both high and low concurrently.

Full real record (hypothesis, verification, refutation): 2026-08-30-janusian-cell-biology.md

Ecology × Materials Science ADJACENT ACTIVE +30 ▸
Domains: Ecology × Materials Science
🧬 Bisociative🗺️ Frontier Research Group💀 Refuted🔬 Actively Researched

Score breakdown (+30 pts)

  • Phase 1 self-report (4/5): not scored — near-zero predictive signal, see Failure 5
  • Phase 2 ADJACENT_ACTIVE: +30
  • Adversarial refutation REFUTED, unanimous (0-of-3 survive): -15
  • independently confirmed (3 separate agents, full agreement)
  • Actively researched, most recent evidence 2017 (9y old): +15

🔬 Independent Research Matches

These studies provide real, specific evidence of research into the application of phase transition models in predator-prey dynamics, aligning with the claim that mathematical models predicting population oscillations in predator-prey systems can also predict behaviors in materials undergoing phase transitions.

  • Additive noise driven phase transitions in a predator-prey system (2017) — Canrong Tian, Ling Lin, Lai Zhang
    This study formulates a predator-prey model incorporating additive noise and investigates its impact on phase transitions, revealing that noise can induce transitions from spatially homogeneous states to regular spiral waves and further to spiral turbulence.
  • Phase transitions in predator-prey systems (2012) — Seido Nagano, Yusuke Maeda
    The authors present a phase diagram for a predator-prey system, demonstrating that stable lattice structures emerge under specific conditions, such as limited prey diffusion and higher carrying capacity, leading to spatially organized patterns.
  • Phase transitions and oscillations in a lattice prey-predator model (2001) — Tibor Antal, Michel Droz
    This research introduces a three-state lattice model for a two-dimensional prey-predator system, revealing that the system exhibits phase transitions between pure prey and coexistence phases, with temporal and spatial oscillations present in the coexistence phase.

Notes

The search results reveal studies on predator-prey dynamics exhibiting oscillatory behaviors, such as the Lotka-Volterra model, and phase transitions in materials science, like oscillatory reactions in catalytic processes. These findings suggest that both domains can exhibit oscillatory behaviors and phase transitions, potentially allowing for a mapping between them.

Full real record (hypothesis, verification, refutation): 2026-08-29-ecology-x-materials-science.md

🎭 Janusian🏛️ Established Department🔬 Actively Researched

Score breakdown (+20 pts)

🔬 Independent Research Matches

The cited studies provide empirical evidence that common mycorrhizal networks (CMNs) can simultaneously enhance nutrient uptake and foster competitive interactions among plants, aligning with the specific claim. These studies demonstrate that CMNs can both benefit plant health and create competitive disadvantages, supporting the falsifiable prediction that certain plant species may exhibit enhanced growth while others decline in the presence of CMNs.

  • Common mycorrhizal networks amplify competition by preferential mineral nutrient allocation to large host plants (2016) — Joanna Weremijewicz, Leonel da Silveira Lobo O'Reilly Sternberg, David P Janos
    This study demonstrates that common mycorrhizal networks (CMNs) can enhance nutrient uptake for plants while simultaneously amplifying competition by preferentially allocating mineral nutrients to larger host plants, thus supporting the claim that CMNs can both benefit plant health and create competitive disadvantages.
  • Common arbuscular mycorrhizal networks amplify competition for phosphorus between seedlings and established plants (2013) — Marie P Merrild, Per Ambus, Søren Rosendahl, Iver Jakobsen
    This research shows that CMNs can intensify competition for phosphorus between seedlings and established plants, indicating that CMNs can simultaneously enhance nutrient uptake and foster competition among plants.
  • Presence and identity of arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi influence competitive interactions between plant species (2007) — Tanja R. Scheublin
    This study investigates how different arbuscular mycorrhizal fungi isolates affect competitive relationships between plant species, providing evidence that CMNs can influence both nutrient uptake and competitive interactions among plants.

Notes

The search results reveal that the exact connection proposed in the hypothesis has already been established in existing research, indicating that the hypothesis is not novel.

Full real record (hypothesis, verification, refutation): 2026-08-31-janusian-ecology.md

🔬 Independent Research Matches

The cited studies directly address the interplay between herd immunity thresholds and the variability in vaccination campaign effectiveness, leading to unpredictable outbreaks even when populations appear to meet the HIT.

  • Dangers of vaccine refusal near the herd immunity threshold: a modelling study (2015) — Nina H. Fefferman, Elena N. Naumova
    This study examines how vaccine refusal near the herd immunity threshold can lead to unpredictable outbreaks, highlighting the variability in vaccination campaign effectiveness.
  • Herd Immunity and Epidemic Size in Networks with Vaccination Homophily (2021) — Takayuki Hiraoka, Abbas K. Rizi, Mikko Kivelä, Jari Saramäki
    This research investigates how homophily in vaccination behavior affects the herd immunity threshold and epidemic size, demonstrating that variations in vaccination patterns can lead to unpredictable outbreaks.

Notes

These studies provide evidence that the HIT is not a fixed value but varies due to individual differences in susceptibility and exposure. This variability can lead to unpredictable outbreaks, even in populations that appear to meet the HIT.

These studies provide empirical evidence supporting the claim that increased collaborative creative input can lead to significant improvements in the quality and quantity of creative outputs.

  • Collaborative Musical Creativity: How Ensembles Coordinate Spontaneity (2018) — Williamon, A., Davidson, J. W., & Faulkner, R.
    This study examines how musical ensembles coordinate spontaneity, highlighting the relationship between collaborative input and the quality of creative outputs.
  • Collaborative Creativity: A Complex Systems Model with Distributed Affect (2011) — Aragon, C. R., & Williams, A.
    This paper proposes a model for creativity in distributed groups, emphasizing the role of collaborative input in enhancing creative outputs.
  • Incentives and Creativity in Groups—Experimental Evidence on Creative Processes and Dimensions (2026) — Sarrazin, E.
    This experimental study investigates how different incentives affect creative processes in groups, focusing on the relationship between collaborative input and the quality and quantity of creative outputs.

Notes

Threshold models in epidemiology, such as those in occupational settings, describe the point at which exposure to a risk factor leads to a significant increase in disease incidence. Similarly, the intelligence-creativity threshold hypothesis suggests that intelligence positively influences creativity up to a certain point, beyond which the relationship weakens. These models highlight the importance of critical thresholds in both health and creative performance.

The cited studies provide real, specific evidence that gravitational lensing can induce diffraction effects in both gravitational and electromagnetic waves, supporting the claim that the bending of light in gravitational lensing is governed by principles similar to those in diffraction patterns.

  • Detecting lensing-induced diffraction in astrophysical gravitational waves (2018) — Liang Dai, Shun-Sheng Li, Barak Zackay, Shude Mao, Youjun Lu
    This study investigates how gravitational lensing can induce diffraction effects in gravitational waves, demonstrating that gravitational lensing can lead to diffraction patterns in waveforms.
  • Diffraction of electromagnetic waves by an extended gravitational lens (2021) — Slava G. Turyshev, Viktor T. Toth
    This research examines the diffraction of electromagnetic waves by an extended gravitational lens, showing that gravitational lensing can cause diffraction effects in electromagnetic waves.

    This paper revisits the diffraction integral in gravitational lensing, providing a systematic approach to evaluate diffraction effects beyond the eikonal approximation.

Notes

Gravitational lensing involves the bending of light due to massive objects, as predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity. This phenomenon is mathematically described by the deflection angle formula: α = 4GM/(c²b), where G is the gravitational constant, M is the mass of the lensing object, c is the speed of light, and b is the impact parameter. In optics, diffraction patterns arise when light encounters obstacles or slits, leading to constructive and destructive interference. The angular position of the m-th diffraction minimum is given by: sin(θ) = mλ/d, where λ is the wavelength of light, d is the distance between slits, and m is the diffraction order. While both phenomena involve the bending of light, the underlying causes and mathematical treatments differ significantly.

The provided matches demonstrate that researchers have explored the mathematical analogy between the Black-Scholes equation and diffusion equations, particularly in the context of option pricing and financial modeling. These studies validate the specific claim regarding the shared probabilistic spread over time influenced by initial conditions and external factors in both fields.

  • Solution of the Black Scholes Equation Using the Green's Function of the Diffusion Equation (1999) — Dennis Silverman
    This work demonstrates how the Black-Scholes equation, fundamental in financial pricing, can be solved using methods from the diffusion equation, highlighting the mathematical analogy between the two.
  • On modified Black–Scholes equation (2004) — Not specified
    This paper discusses the relationship between the Black–Scholes equation and the diffusion equation, proposing a modified Black–Scholes equation based on the telegraph equation, which is more suitable from several points of view.
  • Diffusion Equation and Monte Carlo (2007) — Anders Eskil Österling
    This work introduces the Brownian motion in the context of the diffusion equation and connects it to the Black-Scholes model, providing insights into the relationship between diffusion processes and financial modeling.

Notes

The Black-Scholes equation, a parabolic partial differential equation, describes the price of a European option as a function of the underlying asset price and time. The Fokker-Planck equation governs the time evolution of probability densities for Markovian stochastic processes, incorporating drift and diffusion effects. The Black-Scholes equation can be viewed as a specific instance of the Fokker-Planck equation, with the option price serving as the probability density function and the underlying asset price as the state variable. The Boltzmann equation, a generalization of the Fokker-Planck equation, has been applied in finance to model the distribution of asset prices and option pricing, highlighting the connection between diffusion processes in physics and financial markets.

  • Detecting lensing-induced diffraction in astrophysical gravitational waves (2018) — Liang Dai, Shun-Sheng Li, Barak Zackay, Shude Mao, Youjun Lu
    This study investigates how gravitational lensing can induce diffraction effects in gravitational waves, demonstrating that gravitational lensing can lead to diffraction patterns in waveforms.
  • Diffraction of electromagnetic waves by an extended gravitational lens (2021) — Slava G. Turyshev, Viktor T. Toth

Notes

Gravitational lensing involves the bending of light due to massive objects, as predicted by Einstein's theory of general relativity. This phenomenon is mathematically described by the deflection angle formula: α = 4GM/(c²b), where G is the gravitational constant, M is the mass of the lensing object, c is the speed of light, and b is the impact parameter. In optics, diffraction patterns arise when light encounters obstacles or slits, leading to constructive and destructive interference. The angular position of the m-th diffraction minimum is given by: sin(θ) = mλ/d, where λ is the wavelength of light, d is the distance between slits, and m is the diffraction order. While both phenomena involve the bending of light, the underlying causes and mathematical treatments differ significantly.

  • Solution of the Black Scholes Equation Using the Green's Function of the Diffusion Equation (1999) — Dennis Silverman
    This work demonstrates how the Black-Scholes equation, fundamental in financial pricing, can be solved using methods from the diffusion equation, highlighting the mathematical analogy between the two.

The Black-Scholes equation can be viewed as a specific instance of the Fokker-Planck equation, with the option price serving as the probability density function and the underlying asset price as the state variable. The Boltzmann equation, a generalization of the Fokker-Planck equation, has been applied in finance to model the distribution of asset prices and option pricing, highlighting the connection between diffusion processes in physics and financial markets.

    • Manipulator Inverse Kinematics for Untimed End-Effector Trajectories With Ordinary Singularities (1992) — Jon Kieffer
      This paper presents an algorithm for solving inverse kinematics problems in six-degree-of-freedom manipulators, addressing both regular configurations and specific singularities where the end effector must pause during trajectory execution.
    • Differential Topology of the Inverse Kinematic Problem for Redundant Robot Manipulators (1991) — Krzysztof Tchoń
      This study systematically applies singularity theory to robotics, proposing normal forms as candidate models for manipulator kinematics and examining singularities and bifurcation diagrams relevant to inverse kinematics in redundant manipulators.
    • Inverse Kinematic Solutions With Singularity Robustness for Robot Manipulator Control (1986) — Yoshihiko Nakamura, Hideo Hanafusa
      This paper introduces the Singularity Robust Inverse (SR-inverse) as an alternative to the pseudoinverse of the Jacobian matrix, providing solutions even at or near singular points, thereby addressing the issue of physical constraints in inverse kinematics.

    Notes

    The search results provide detailed explanations of inverse kinematics (IK) limitations, joint constraints, and singularities in robotic arms. For instance, singularities occur when the Jacobian matrix loses rank, leading to configurations where the robot cannot move in certain directions, resulting in infinite joint velocities or unbounded end-effector forces. (mtsu.pressbooks.pub) Additionally, joint constraints are rotational limitations on the joints of an artificial system, which can be implemented in various ways to restrict movement. (en.wikipedia.org) These findings support the hypothesis that a robotic arm can achieve a desired end-effector position through inverse kinematics but may be unable to reach certain positions due to physical constraints and singularities.

Skinner, posits that behavior is shaped by its consequences—reinforcements or punishments—that increase or decrease the likelihood of a behavior's recurrence.       This study proposes that chunking is a rational strategy for lossy data compression in visual working memory, facilitating performance improvements for capacity-limited systems and increasing effective storage capacity at the expense of recall precision.

This evidence supports the hypothesis that both the limited capacity of working memory and the effective expansion through chunking can simultaneously apply to the same cognitive tasks.

    Score breakdown (+40 pts)

    • Actively researched, most recent evidence 2024 (2y old — a live, current research thread): +25

    🔬 Independent Research Match

    The identified study directly investigates the coexistence of rational and irrational players within a game-theoretic framework, introducing the $b1$-Rational Nash Equilibrium (RNE) to model this interaction. The findings indicate that rational players can leverage the behavior of irrational players to attain higher utility, providing empirical evidence for the proposed mechanism.

    • Balancing rationality and social influence: Alpha-rational Nash equilibrium in games with herding (2024) — Khushboo Agarwal, Konstantin Avrachenkov, Veeraruna Kavitha, Raghupati Vyas
      This study introduces the concept of the $b1$-Rational Nash Equilibrium (RNE), where a fraction of rational players coexist with irrational players exhibiting herding behavior. The analysis demonstrates that rational players can benefit from the presence of irrational players, leading to equilibria where rational players may achieve higher utility than in classical settings, thus addressing the simultaneous presence of rational and irrational players in negotiations.

    Notes

    The Nash Bargaining Solution (NBS) is a foundational concept in game theory that identifies a unique, fair outcome for two parties negotiating a mutually beneficial agreement. It is based on four key axioms: efficiency, symmetry, invariance to utility scale, and independence of irrelevant alternatives. These principles ensure that the solution is both rational and equitable. (umbrex.com)

    In real-world negotiations, however, players often exhibit behaviors that deviate from strict rationality. Such behaviors are typically categorized as irrational or bounded rationality, where decision-making is influenced by cognitive limitations, emotions, or social factors. These deviations can lead to outcomes that differ from those predicted by the NBS. For instance, negotiators may accept less favorable terms due to emotional attachments or social pressures, even when more advantageous agreements are available. (time.com)

    The interplay between rational and irrational behaviors in negotiations has been explored in various studies. Research indicates that the presence of irrational players can alter the dynamics of bargaining situations, potentially leading to outcomes that neither purely rational nor purely irrational players would predict in isolation. This suggests that the NBS, while providing a foundational framework, may not fully capture the complexities of real-world negotiations where human behavior introduces additional layers of unpredictability. (direct.mit.edu)

    In summary, while the Nash Bargaining Solution offers a theoretical model for fair negotiation outcomes, actual negotiations often involve a mix of rational and irrational behaviors. This blend can result in agreements that differ from those anticipated by the NBS, highlighting the need for models that account for the full spectrum of human decision-making in bargaining scenarios.

    Full real record (hypothesis, verification, refutation): 2026-08-31-janusian-game-theory-2.md

      This paper develops a taxonomy of institutional change explanations, delineating the scope of path dependence and its interaction with other change mechanisms, addressing the coexistence of historical path dependence and independent evolution.
    • Path Constitution Analysis: A Methodology for Understanding Path Dependence and Path Creation (2014) — Jörg Sydow, Arnold Windeler, Gordon Müller-Seitz, Knut Lange
      This study introduces 'Path Constitution Analysis' to understand both path dependence and path creation, providing a methodology that accounts for the simultaneous influence of historical decisions and independent contexts on institutional change.
    • The Path of Most Persistence: An Evolutionary Perspective on Path Dependence and Dynamic Capabilities (2011) — Jean-Philippe Vergne, Rodolphe Durand
      This paper extends the dynamic capability view by introducing an evolutionary perspective, specifying the underlying selection mechanisms of path dependence in internal and external firm environments, addressing the coexistence of path dependence and independent evolution.

Rixen and Viola (2015) develop a taxonomy of institutional change explanations, addressing the scope of path dependence relative to other change explanations.     3. Relational Contracts: These are long-term agreements built around ongoing business relationships rather than fixed obligations. They allow for flexibility and adaptation, acknowledging that not all future scenarios can be predicted at the outset. (legalclarity.org)

    4. The Problem of Creative Collaboration: This work explores how informal rules and relational contracts can facilitate and organize collaboration in creative industries, highlighting the importance of adaptable agreements in creative processes. (papers.ssrn.com)

    These frameworks collectively support the concept of "Creative Contractuality," emphasizing the need for flexible, adaptable agreements that evolve with the creative process.

    The sources provide evidence supporting the claim that creole languages develop from a pidgin stage and arise directly from the interaction of native speakers simultaneously for the same community.     Score breakdown (+45 pts)

    • Phase 1 self-report (4/5): not scored — near-zero predictive signal, see Failure 5
    • Phase 2 ADJACENT_ACTIVE: +30
    • Actively researched, most recent evidence 2023 (3y old): +15

    🔬 Independent Research Matches

    The cited studies employ models and optimization techniques inspired by chemical reaction networks to analyze and improve urban traffic flow, directly addressing the proposed mechanism.

    • Unraveling reaction-diffusion-like dynamics in urban congestion propagation: Insights from a large-scale road network (2020) — Leonardo Bellocchi, Nikolas Geroliminis
      This study develops a dynamic model combining reaction and diffusion terms to simulate traffic congestion propagation in urban networks, revealing self-organized patterns akin to chemical reaction networks.
    • Global efficiency and network structure of urban traffic flows: A percolation-based empirical analysis (2023) — Yungi Kwon, Jung-Hoon Jung, Young-Ho Eom
      This research employs percolation theory to analyze the global efficiency and network structure of urban traffic flows, drawing parallels to concepts in chemical reaction networks.
    • Designing reduced congestion road networks via an elitist adaptive chemical reaction optimization (2022) — Not specified
      This paper proposes an elitist adaptive chemical reaction optimization approach to redesign urban traffic networks, aiming to reduce congestion.

    Notes

    The Traffic Reaction Model (TRM) introduces a kinetic compartmental approach to road traffic modeling, drawing parallels between traffic flow dynamics and chemical reaction networks. This model employs finite volume discretization schemes for LWR-type first-order traffic flow models, resulting in systems of ordinary differential equations (ODEs) that are formally equivalent to kinetic systems used in chemical reaction networks. The TRM offers a novel compartmental interpretation of traffic models, utilizing kinetic theory to derive dynamical properties such as persistence and Lyapunov stability for specific road configurations. (sciencedirect.com)

    A measure-theoretic approach to traffic flow optimization on networks considers optimal control problems for measure-valued nonlinear transport equations describing traffic flow on networks. The objective is to minimize or maximize macroscopic quantities, such as traffic volume or average speed, by controlling a few agents, such as smart traffic lights and automated cars. This approach allows for the study of local and non-local driver interactions and considers control variables as additional measures interacting with the drivers' distribution. (researchgate.net)

    Percolation theory provides a mathematical framework to study connectivity and robustness in systems where elements can be in one of two states—open or closed. Applied to urban traffic, this approach treats roads and intersections as a network of edges and nodes, and congestion or failures as the removal or reduction of capacity on those edges. By analyzing how clusters of congested or inoperative roads grow and coalesce, researchers can identify critical points—percolation thresholds—beyond which the network fragments and large-scale gridlock ensues. (nature.com)

    Full real record (hypothesis, verification, refutation): 2026-08-31-urban-planning-x-physical-chemical-reaction-networks.md
